about: Constitutional Law (Paper 11) is one of the four Part IA papers in the Cambridge Law Tripos, taught through lectures and fortnightly supervisions and assessed mainly by an examination at the end of the year. The Faculty describes it as covering how power is allocated among the UK's institutions and how they relate to citizens: separation of powers and the rule of law, legislative authority, the multi-layered constitution (the EU and Brexit, and devolution), the accountability of Parliament and the executive, judicial review and the UK's human rights framework. This pack follows that list, splitting the multi-layered constitution into two topics.
topics: Separation of powers and the rule of law
The multi-layered constitution: the EU and Brexit
Parliament and the accountability of the executive

notes.h: The UK constitution, separation of powers and the rule of law
notes.body:
The UK has no single codified constitutional document. Its constitution is found in statutes (e.g. the Bill of Rights 1689, the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the Human Rights Act 1998, the devolution Acts, the Constitutional Reform Act 2005), common law (including the royal prerogative), conventions, and works of authority. Because so much rests on ordinary statute and convention, it is often called "political" or "flexible", though the courts increasingly speak of constitutional principles and constitutional statutes.

Separation of powers
- Montesquieu (The Spirit of the Laws, 1748) argued that liberty requires legislative, executive and judicial power to be held by different bodies.
- The UK has only a partial separation. Ministers sit in Parliament and the government normally controls the Commons; Walter Bagehot (The English Constitution, 1867) called the close union of executive and legislature through the Cabinet the "efficient secret" of the constitution.
- The strongest separation is the independence of the judiciary. The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (CRA) ended the Lord Chancellor's role as head of the judiciary (the Lord Chief Justice now heads the judiciary of England and Wales), created the Supreme Court (which opened in October 2009) to replace the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords, set up the Judicial Appointments Commission, and imposed a duty on ministers to uphold judicial independence (s 3).
- Cases: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Fire Brigades Union [1995] 2 AC 513 (a minister cannot use the prerogative to frustrate a statutory scheme Parliament has enacted); Duport Steels v Sirs [1980] 1 WLR 142 (judges must not substitute their policy views for Parliament's); R (Miller) v Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General [2019] UKSC 41 (courts protect Parliament's ability to perform its functions).

The rule of law
- Dicey (Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution, 1885): no punishment except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary courts; equality of all before the ordinary law; and constitutional rights as the product of ordinary court decisions.
- Joseph Raz ("The Rule of Law and its Virtue", 1977) gave a formal account: law should be prospective, open, clear, stable and applied by independent courts; it is not the same as the rule of good law.
- Lord Bingham (The Rule of Law, 2010) set out eight principles, including accessibility of law, equality, protection of fundamental rights, access to justice, and compliance with international law. This is a "thicker", more substantive conception.
- The CRA 2005, s 1, provides that the Act does not adversely affect the existing constitutional principle of the rule of law.

Key cases
- Entick v Carrington (1765) 19 St Tr 1030: officials need legal authority to interfere with property; the Secretary of State's warrant to search Entick's house and seize his papers had no basis in law, and claims of state necessity could not supply one.
- M v Home Office [1994] 1 AC 377: ministers can be found in contempt of court.
- R (Unison) v Lord Chancellor [2017] UKSC 51: employment tribunal fees were unlawful because they effectively prevented access to justice, which is inherent in the rule of law.
- R (Evans) v Attorney General [2015] UKSC 21: a ministerial certificate overriding a tribunal decision to disclose Prince Charles's letters was unlawful; the majority stressed that an executive override of a judicial decision cuts across the rule of law.

Exam tips: be ready to discuss whether the UK's partial separation of powers is a weakness or a deliberate feature, and to use cases as evidence of the courts' approach to the rule of law. State which conception of the rule of law you are using.

Dicey's orthodox account
Parliament (the King, Lords and Commons acting together) has the right to make or unmake any law, and no person or body is recognised as having a right to override or set aside its legislation. Three corollaries follow:
- Parliament can legislate on any subject (even with extra-territorial effect).
- Courts cannot question the validity of an Act. The enrolled bill rule: Edinburgh and Dalkeith Railway v Wauchope (1842) 8 Cl & F 710; Pickin v British Railways Board [1974] AC 765.
- Parliament cannot bind its successors. A later inconsistent Act impliedly repeals an earlier one: Vauxhall Estates v Liverpool Corporation [1932] 1 KB 733; Ellen Street Estates v Minister of Health [1934] 1 KB 590.

The Parliament Acts and Jackson
The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 allow most public bills to become law without the Lords' consent after a delay (about one year), and money bills after one month. In R (Jackson) v Attorney General [2005] UKHL 56, the House of Lords held the 1949 Act (which was itself passed under the 1911 procedure) and the Hunting Act 2004 valid. Obiter dicta questioned absolute sovereignty:
- Lord Steyn suggested courts might not uphold an Act abolishing judicial review or the ordinary role of the courts.
- Lord Hope said parliamentary sovereignty is no longer, if it ever was, absolute, and that the rule of law is the ultimate controlling factor.
- Some judges accepted that Parliament could redefine itself for certain purposes (a "manner and form" view), as in Attorney-General for New South Wales v Trethowan [1932] AC 526 (in a non-sovereign legislature).

Constitutional statutes
- Thoburn v Sunderland City Council [2002] EWHC 195 (Admin): Laws LJ said "constitutional statutes" (e.g. Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights, the European Communities Act 1972, the Human Rights Act 1998) cannot be impliedly repealed; only express words or clear intention will do.
- R (HS2 Action Alliance) v Secretary of State for Transport [2014] UKSC 3: the Supreme Court suggested there may be fundamental principles that even EU law could not override without Parliament clearly intending it.

Ouster clauses and legality
- Anisminic v Foreign Compensation Commission [1969] 2 AC 147: an ouster clause did not protect a "purported" determination vitiated by error of law, which was a nullity.
- R (Privacy International) v Investigatory Powers Tribunal [2019] UKSC 22: the ouster in s 67(8) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 did not prevent review of the tribunal's errors of law. Lord Carnwath (for the plurality) said obiter that it is ultimately for the courts to decide the limits that the rule of law imposes on attempts to exclude review.
- The principle of legality (R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Simms [2000] 2 AC 115): Parliament must use clear words to override fundamental rights; general words are read subject to them.

Sovereignty and other layers
- EU membership: Factortame (No 2) [1991] 1 AC 603 disapplied an Act of Parliament inconsistent with EU law, explained as Parliament's own choice in the European Communities Act 1972.
- Devolution and the HRA expressly preserve Westminster's power (Scotland Act 1998, s 28(7); HRA s 4(6)).

Exam tips: essays usually ask whether sovereignty is still the "bedrock" of the constitution. Set out Dicey, then test it against Jackson, Thoburn, HS2, Privacy International, EU membership and devolution, and reach a view on whether these are legal limits or political constraints.

notes.h: The EU, Brexit and the constitution
notes.body:
Membership (1973 to 2020)
- The European Communities Act 1972 (ECA) gave EU law effect in UK law: s 2(1) made directly effective EU law enforceable, and s 2(4) required other legislation to be read and take effect subject to it.
- R v Secretary of State for Transport, ex p Factortame (No 2) [1991] 1 AC 603: the House of Lords disapplied parts of the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 that conflicted with EU law. Lord Bridge explained this as a limitation Parliament had voluntarily accepted in 1972.
- Thoburn treated the ECA as a constitutional statute immune from implied repeal, and the European Union Act 2011, s 18, stated that EU law took effect only by virtue of Acts of Parliament.

Leaving: Miller I
R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union [2017] UKSC 5:
- The government could not use the prerogative to give notice of withdrawal under Article 50 TEU, because withdrawal would change domestic law and remove rights that Parliament had created. An Act of Parliament was required, and the European Union (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017 followed.
- The Sewel convention (that Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without consent) is a political convention that courts cannot enforce, despite its statutory recognition in the Scotland Act 1998, s 28(8).

The withdrawal legislation
- The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 (EUWA) repealed the ECA on exit day (31 January 2020), though its effect was saved during the implementation period, and created "retained EU law", which took effect at the end of 2020, so that the statute book would continue to work.
- The European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020 implemented the Withdrawal Agreement, including a transition (implementation) period ending on 31 December 2020. EUWA s 7A gives the Withdrawal Agreement, including the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland (amended by the Windsor Framework in 2023), effect in domestic law.
- The EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement governs the future relationship and was given effect by the European Union (Future Relationship) Act 2020.
- The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 abolished the principle of supremacy of EU law and the general principles of EU law in domestic law from the end of 2023, and renamed retained EU law "assimilated law". Courts now have more freedom to depart from retained EU case law.

Constitutional significance
- Brexit showed both the strength of parliamentary sovereignty (Parliament chose to join and to leave) and the courts' role in policing the boundary between prerogative and statute (Miller I, and Miller II on prorogation in 2019).
- Re Allister's Application for Judicial Review [2023] UKSC 5: the Northern Ireland Protocol, given effect by EUWA s 7A, lawfully modified the trade provisions of the Acts of Union of 1800, because Parliament can amend or modify constitutional statutes by clear words.
- Brexit put strain on devolution: the UK Withdrawal from the European Union (Legal Continuity) (Scotland) Bill reference [2018] UKSC 64 and the UK Internal Market Act 2020 raised questions about Westminster's power over devolved matters.
- The referendum of 23 June 2016 raised questions about the relationship between direct democracy and representative parliamentary democracy; the referendum was advisory in law.

Exam tips: avoid simply narrating Brexit. Use it to examine sovereignty, prerogative power, conventions and devolution, citing Factortame, Miller I and Allister precisely.

notes.h: Devolution: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
notes.body:
Devolution transfers legislative and executive power from Westminster to institutions in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, without giving up Westminster's legal sovereignty. The arrangements are asymmetric.

Scotland (Scotland Act 1998)
- The Scottish Parliament may legislate on anything not reserved to Westminster (a "reserved powers" model). Reserved matters, such as the Union, defence, foreign affairs and much of macroeconomic policy, are listed in Schedule 5. Section 29 sets out legislative competence; an Act outside competence "is not law".
- Section 28(7): devolution does not affect the power of the UK Parliament to make laws for Scotland.
- Section 28(8) (added by the Scotland Act 2016): Westminster will "not normally" legislate on devolved matters without the Scottish Parliament's consent (the Sewel convention).
- Section 63A: the Scottish Parliament and Government are a permanent part of the UK's constitutional arrangements and will not be abolished except after a referendum.
- Section 33 allows bills to be referred to the Supreme Court; s 35 allows the Secretary of State to block a bill in certain cases. The first s 35 order (January 2023) blocked the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill, and the Court of Session upheld it in December 2023.

Wales (Government of Wales Act 2006)
- The Senedd (renamed by the Senedd and Elections (Wales) Act 2020) has full law-making powers in devolved areas. The Wales Act 2017 moved Wales to a reserved powers model from 2018.
- Equivalent provisions recognise permanence and the Sewel convention.
- The Senedd Cymru (Members and Elections) Act 2024 enlarged the Senedd to 96 members with a closed-list proportional system from the 2026 election.

Northern Ireland (Northern Ireland Act 1998)
- Based on the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement (1998): power-sharing between unionist and nationalist communities, with a First Minister and deputy First Minister who hold office jointly.
- Matters are excepted (permanently with Westminster), reserved (may be transferred) or transferred.
- Section 1: Northern Ireland remains part of the UK unless a majority of its people vote otherwise in a border poll.
- The institutions have been suspended or collapsed several times, most recently between 2022 and early 2024.

Key Supreme Court decisions
- Miller I [2017] UKSC 5: the Sewel convention, even when written into statute, is not legally enforceable.
- Continuity Bill reference [2018] UKSC 64: most of the Scottish Bill was within competence when passed, but later Westminster legislation (EUWA 2018, protected from modification) meant several provisions could not take effect.
- UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Bill reference [2021] UKSC 42: provisions that would have restricted Westminster's own power to legislate for Scotland were outside competence because they would modify s 28(7).
- Reference re Scottish Independence Referendum Bill [2022] UKSC 31: a bill for an advisory independence referendum "relates to" the reserved matters of the Union and the UK Parliament, so it was outside Holyrood's competence.
- AXA General Insurance v HM Advocate [2011] UKSC 46: Acts of the Scottish Parliament are not reviewable for Wednesbury unreasonableness, but they are subject to the rule of law and Convention rights.

England and intergovernmental relations
England has no devolved legislature. Intergovernmental relations were restructured after a 2022 review, and the UK Internal Market Act 2020 (a protected enactment) limits how far devolved rules can restrict trade within the UK.

Exam tips: distinguish legal power (s 28(7)) from political constraint (Sewel). Use the references as evidence of how the Supreme Court reads devolution statutes: as ordinary statutes, interpreted with an eye to the constitutional settlement.

In the UK the executive (the Prime Minister, Cabinet and ministers, supported by the civil service) is drawn from and depends on the confidence of the House of Commons. Accountability is therefore largely political, enforced through Parliament and conventions, with legal control via the courts in the background.

Conventions
Conventions are binding rules of political practice that courts recognise but do not enforce (Attorney-General v Jonathan Cape [1976] QB 752; Miller I [2017]).
- Sir Ivor Jennings's test: are there precedents, do the actors believe they are bound, and is there a reason for the rule?
- Examples: the King gives Royal Assent to bills passed by Parliament; the King acts on ministerial advice; the Prime Minister must command the confidence of the Commons; the Salisbury convention (the Lords do not block manifesto bills at second reading); the Sewel convention.
- Many are written down in the Cabinet Manual (2011) and the Ministerial Code, but that does not make them law.

Ministerial responsibility
- Collective responsibility: ministers are bound by Cabinet decisions and must support them publicly or resign; Cabinet discussions are confidential; the government must keep the confidence of the Commons. It can be suspended (e.g. the 2016 EU referendum).
- Individual responsibility: ministers answer to Parliament for their departments and must not knowingly mislead Parliament (Ministerial Code). Resignation for departmental failures is rare; resignations more often follow personal misconduct.

Parliamentary scrutiny
- Questions: oral questions including Prime Minister's Questions, and written questions.
- Debates, opposition days and urgent questions.
- Departmental select committees (established 1979); since 2010 their chairs are elected by the whole House. The Public Accounts Committee scrutinises spending, supported by the National Audit Office. The Liaison Committee questions the Prime Minister.
- The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (Parliamentary Commissioner Act 1967) investigates maladministration, with complaints referred by MPs.
- Parliamentary privilege: Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689 protects freedom of speech and proceedings in Parliament from being questioned in any court; it does not protect ordinary criminality such as fraudulent expense claims (R v Chaytor [2010] UKSC 52).

The House of Lords
- The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 limit the Lords to delaying most bills (about one year) and money bills (one month).
- The House of Lords Act 1999 removed most hereditary peers, leaving 92. The House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026) removed the remaining hereditary peers at the end of that parliamentary session (the provision came into force on 29 April 2026).

The royal prerogative
- Residual common law powers of the Crown, mostly exercised by ministers: treaty-making, foreign affairs, deployment of the armed forces, mercy, honours, and (formerly) prorogation and dissolution.
- No new prerogatives can be created (BBC v Johns [1965] Ch 32), and the King cannot change the law by proclamation (Case of Proclamations (1611)).
- Where statute covers the same ground, the prerogative is displaced (Attorney-General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel [1920] AC 508), and it cannot be used to frustrate a statute (Fire Brigades Union [1995]).
- Prerogative powers are reviewable (CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374), though some subject matter is non-justiciable.
- Miller II [2019] UKSC 41: a prorogation that frustrates or prevents, without reasonable justification, Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions is unlawful. The 2019 prorogation was void.
- The Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011, revived the prerogative to dissolve Parliament, tried to make its exercise non-justiciable (s 3), and provides for automatic dissolution five years after a Parliament first meets.
- The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 put the civil service on a statutory footing and requires most treaties to be laid before Parliament for 21 sitting days before ratification.

Exam tips: assess how effective these mechanisms are in practice, given executive dominance of the Commons, and show where courts have stepped in (Miller I and II) and where they have refused (enforcing conventions).

Judicial review (JR) allows the High Court (Administrative Court) to review the lawfulness of decisions by public bodies. It is concerned with the legality of the decision-making process, not the merits: the court asks whether the decision was lawfully made, not whether it was right.

Procedure
- Claims are brought under the Senior Courts Act 1981, s 31, and Civil Procedure Rules Part 54, with a permission stage.
- Time limit: promptly, and in any event within three months of the grounds arising (CPR 54.5), with shorter limits in planning and procurement.
- Standing: a "sufficient interest in the matter" (s 31(3)); interpreted generously for public interest groups (IRC v National Federation of Self-Employed and Small Businesses [1982] AC 617; R v Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, ex p World Development Movement [1995] 1 WLR 386).
- Amenability: public bodies and bodies exercising public functions, judged by the source and nature of the power (R v Panel on Take-overs and Mergers, ex p Datafin [1987] QB 815).
- Relief must be refused if it is highly likely the outcome would not have been substantially different without the conduct complained of (s 31(2A), added in 2015), unless there is exceptional public interest.

Grounds of review (Lord Diplock in CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374)
1. Illegality: the decision-maker must understand and give effect to the law regulating its power.
- Acting outside the powers conferred (ultra vires).
- Using a power for an improper purpose, or to frustrate the policy of the Act (Padfield v Minister of Agriculture [1968] AC 997).
- Taking into account irrelevant considerations or ignoring relevant ones.
- Fettering discretion by applying a rigid policy, or unlawfully delegating it.
- Errors of law (Anisminic [1969] 2 AC 147).
2. Irrationality: a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it (Associated Provincial Picture Houses v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223), or "so outrageous in its defiance of logic or accepted moral standards" (CCSU). Intensity varies with context: closer scrutiny where fundamental rights are at stake (Pham v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2015] UKSC 19; Kennedy v Charity Commission [2014] UKSC 20).
3. Procedural impropriety:
- Failure to follow statutory procedures.
- The right to a fair hearing, whose content varies with context (Ridge v Baldwin [1964] AC 40; R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Doody [1994] 1 AC 531).
- The rule against bias: automatic disqualification for a direct interest (R v Bow Street Magistrate, ex p Pinochet (No 2) [2000] 1 AC 119); otherwise, whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill [2001] UKHL 67).
- Legitimate expectations, procedural or substantive: R v North and East Devon Health Authority, ex p Coughlan [2001] QB 213 (a clear promise of a "home for life" was enforced).
4. Proportionality (Lord Diplock anticipated its possible future adoption): required where Convention rights are engaged under the HRA. The four-stage test in Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2) [2013] UKSC 39: is the objective sufficiently important; is the measure rationally connected to it; could a less intrusive measure have been used; and does the measure strike a fair balance?

Remedies
Quashing orders, prohibiting orders, mandatory orders, declarations, injunctions, and limited damages. The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 added suspended and prospective-only quashing orders (s 29A Senior Courts Act 1981) and ousted review of Upper Tribunal refusals of permission to appeal (reversing R (Cart) v Upper Tribunal [2011] UKSC 28).

Constitutional justification
The "ultra vires" theory says courts enforce Parliament's intention. The common law theory says JR rests on the courts' own constitutional principles (rule of law, fairness). The debate matters for ouster clauses (Privacy International [2019]).

Exam tips: in problem questions, deal with procedure (permission, time, standing, amenability) briefly, then work through each ground that the facts raise, and finish with remedies.

notes.h: The Human Rights Act 1998 and the UK human rights framework
notes.body:
The UK ratified the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) in 1951 and has allowed individual petition to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in Strasbourg since 1966. The Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA), in force from 2 October 2000, made most Convention rights enforceable in domestic courts while preserving parliamentary sovereignty.

Key provisions
- s 1 and Schedule 1: the Convention rights given effect (e.g. Article 2 life, Article 3 torture, Article 5 liberty, Article 6 fair trial, Article 8 private and family life, Article 10 expression, Article 14 discrimination).
- s 2: courts must "take into account" Strasbourg case law. In R (Ullah) v Special Adjudicator [2004] UKHL 26, Lord Bingham said courts should keep pace with Strasbourg, "no more, but certainly no less" (the "mirror principle"). Later cases allow departure in some circumstances: R v Horncastle [2009] UKSC 14 (dialogue with Strasbourg) and Manchester City Council v Pinnock [2010] UKSC 45 (follow a clear and constant line of decisions).
- s 3: so far as it is possible to do so, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights. This is a strong interpretive obligation: Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] UKHL 30 read "as his or her wife or husband" to include same-sex partners. But it cannot go against a fundamental feature of the legislation (Re S (Care Order: Implementation of Care Plan) [2002] UKHL 10).
- s 4: if a compatible reading is impossible, higher courts may make a declaration of incompatibility. It does not affect the validity of the Act (s 4(6)), and Parliament and government decide how to respond. Examples: Bellinger v Bellinger [2003] UKHL 21, followed by the Gender Recognition Act 2004; A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 56 (indefinite detention of foreign terrorist suspects), followed by the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005; R (Steinfeld) v Secretary of State for International Development [2018] UKSC 32, followed by opposite-sex civil partnerships.
- s 6: it is unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with Convention rights, unless primary legislation required it (s 6(2)). Core public authorities are always covered; hybrid bodies are covered when performing "functions of a public nature" (s 6(3)(b)): Aston Cantlow PCC v Wallbank [2003] UKHL 37; YL v Birmingham City Council [2007] UKHL 27 (later reversed by statute for publicly arranged care). Courts are public authorities, which gives the HRA some indirect horizontal effect (Campbell v MGN [2004] UKHL 22).
- ss 7 and 8: victims may bring proceedings; damages where necessary for just satisfaction.
- s 10: remedial orders to amend incompatible legislation quickly.
- s 19: ministers must make a statement of compatibility (or state that they cannot) for each government bill.

The HRA and constitutional theory
- The HRA is often described as a "dialogue" or "parliamentary rights" model: courts identify incompatibility, but Parliament has the last word.
- The courts also show deference, or respect for institutional competence, on sensitive moral and social questions: R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice [2014] UKSC 38 (assisted suicide; the majority declined to make a declaration at that time).
- The common law also protects fundamental rights (the principle of legality; Unison [2017]), and some judges have stressed that the HRA is not the only source of rights protection.

Debates and reform
- The Independent Human Rights Act Review reported in December 2021. A Bill of Rights Bill to replace the HRA was introduced in 2022 and withdrawn in 2023.
- The Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 disapplied key HRA provisions for that Act after R (AAA) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2023] UKSC 42 found the Rwanda policy unlawful; it was repealed by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 (s 40), with effect from 2 December 2025.
- Political debate continues about the UK's relationship with the ECHR and the ECtHR, so keep up with current developments.

Exam tips: be precise about the difference between ss 3 and 4, and about the remedies against public authorities under s 6. Essays often ask whether the HRA strikes the right balance between courts and Parliament.

cards.f: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748)
cards.b: Argued liberty requires legislative, executive and judicial power to be held by separate bodies.
The close union of executive and legislature through the Cabinet (The English Constitution, 1867).
s 1: Act does not adversely affect the rule of law; s 3: ministers must uphold judicial independence. It also created the Supreme Court and the JAC.

cards.f: Dicey's three meanings of the rule of law
cards.b: No punishment except for distinct breach of law in ordinary courts; equality before the ordinary law; constitutional rights flow from court decisions.
Eight principles, including accessible law, equality, protection of fundamental rights, access to justice and compliance with international law: a 'thick' conception.
State officials need positive legal authority to interfere with a person's property; the Secretary of State's warrant to search Entick's house and seize his papers was unlawful.
Employment tribunal fees were unlawful because they effectively prevented access to justice, inherent in the rule of law.
Ministers and government departments can be found in contempt of court.
Parliament can make or unmake any law, and no person or body can override or set aside its legislation.

cards.f: Pickin v British Railways Board [1974] AC 765
cards.b: Enrolled bill rule: courts will not investigate how an Act passed through Parliament.

cards.f: Ellen Street Estates v Minister of Health [1934]
cards.b: Parliament cannot bind its successors: a later inconsistent Act impliedly repeals the earlier one.
Parliament Act 1949 and Hunting Act 2004 valid; obiter that sovereignty may not be absolute (Lords Steyn and Hope, Baroness Hale).
Laws LJ: 'constitutional statutes' cannot be impliedly repealed; only express or specific words suffice.
The RIPA s 67(8) ouster did not exclude review for errors of law; obiter that courts decide the rule-of-law limits on ousters.
Fundamental rights cannot be overridden by general words; Parliament must squarely confront what it is doing.
Required other legislation to be construed and have effect subject to directly effective EU law.
The House of Lords disapplied the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 for conflict with EU law, as Parliament had accepted in 1972.

cards.f: R (Miller) v SS for Exiting the EU [2017] UKSC 5
cards.b: Article 50 notice required an Act of Parliament because withdrawal would change domestic law; the Sewel convention is not legally enforceable.
31 January 2020 (11pm UK time); the transition (implementation) period ended on 31 December 2020.
Repealed the ECA 1972 and created retained EU law; s 7A (added 2020) gives effect to the Withdrawal Agreement and NI Protocol.

cards.f: Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023
cards.b: Ended supremacy and general principles of EU law domestically from the end of 2023; renamed retained EU law 'assimilated law'.
The NI Protocol, given effect by EUWA s 7A, lawfully modified the trade provisions of the Acts of Union 1800.
Devolution does not affect the power of the UK Parliament to make laws for Scotland.
Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without consent; recognised in s 28(8) SA 1998 but not legally enforceable (Miller I).
The devolved legislature may legislate on anything not expressly reserved to Westminster (Scotland; Wales since 2018).

cards.f: Scottish Independence Referendum Bill reference [2022] UKSC 31
cards.b: A bill for an advisory independence referendum relates to reserved matters (the Union, the UK Parliament), so is outside Holyrood's competence.
Provisions that would restrict Westminster's power to legislate for Scotland were outside competence as modifying s 28(7).
Northern Ireland remains part of the UK unless a majority of its people vote otherwise in a poll.

cards.f: AXA General Insurance v HM Advocate [2011] UKSC 46
cards.b: Acts of the Scottish Parliament are not reviewable for irrationality but are subject to the rule of law and Convention rights.
Are there precedents? Do the actors believe they are bound? Is there a reason for the rule?
Crossman diaries: courts recognise conventions (Cabinet confidentiality) but protected confidence through equity, not by enforcing the convention.
Ministers publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign; Cabinet confidentiality; government must retain the confidence of the Commons.
Freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court.

cards.f: Attorney-General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel [1920] AC 508
cards.b: Where statute covers the same ground as a prerogative power, the prerogative is displaced.
Prorogation that frustrates Parliament's constitutional functions without reasonable justification is unlawful; the 2019 prorogation was void.

cards.f: Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022
cards.b: Repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011, revived the prerogative of dissolution, and provides for automatic dissolution after five years.
The Lords can delay money bills for one month and most other public bills for about one year.

cards.f: CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374
cards.b: Prerogative powers are reviewable; Lord Diplock's grounds: illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety (and possibly proportionality).
A decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it ([1948] 1 KB 223).

cards.f: Padfield v Minister of Agriculture [1968] AC 997
cards.b: Discretion must be used to promote, not frustrate, the policy and objects of the Act.
Test for apparent bias: would a fair-minded and informed observer conclude there was a real possibility of bias?
Substantive legitimate expectation: a clear promise of a 'home for life' was enforced; breaking it was an abuse of power.
Promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds arising (CPR 54.5), subject to shorter specific limits.
Proportionality: important objective; rational connection; no less intrusive means; fair balance between rights and community interests.
Introduced suspended and prospective-only quashing orders (s 29A SCA 1981) and ousted 'Cart' judicial reviews.
So far as possible, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights.
Higher courts may declare legislation incompatible; this does not affect its validity or operation (s 4(6)).
Unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with Convention rights, unless primary legislation required it (s 6(2)).
s 3 used to read 'as his or her wife or husband' to include same-sex partners for tenancy succession.
Belmarsh: indefinite detention of foreign terrorist suspects was disproportionate and discriminatory; declaration of incompatibility.
The 'mirror principle': keep pace with Strasbourg case law, 'no more, but certainly no less'.
A body performing some 'functions of a public nature' (s 6(3)(b)); bound only for its public acts (Aston Cantlow; YL).

cards.f: R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice [2014] UKSC 38
cards.b: Assisted suicide: majority declined to make a declaration of incompatibility, stressing Parliament's role on the issue.

questions.q: Which statute replaced the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords with the UK Supreme Court?
options: Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010
Senior Courts Act 1981
Human Rights Act 1998
Constitutional Reform Act 2005
questions.why: The CRA 2005 created the Supreme Court (opened 2009). CRAG 2010 deals with the civil service and treaties; the HRA with Convention rights; the Senior Courts Act 1981 with the senior courts of England and Wales.

questions.q: In R (Unison) v Lord Chancellor [2017], why were employment tribunal fees held unlawful?
options: They were irrational under Wednesbury
They breached EU free movement law only
They effectively prevented access to justice, which is inherent in the rule of law
They were not approved by the Lords
questions.why: The Supreme Court emphasised the constitutional right of access to justice: the Fees Order was unlawful under domestic law as well as EU law because of its effect on access to the tribunals. It was not decided on Wednesbury grounds or parliamentary procedure.

questions.q: Explain the difference between formal and substantive conceptions of the rule of law, with reference to Raz and Bingham.
markScheme: Formal (thin): concerned with how law is made and its form (prospective, clear, stable, open, applied by independent courts)
Raz (1977): rule of law is a virtue of law but not the rule of good law; compatible with unjust content
Substantive (thick): includes protection of fundamental rights
Bingham (2010): eight principles including fundamental rights and compliance with international law
Evaluation: thin view is clearer and more neutral; thick view captures more but merges with justice
questions.modelAnswer: Formal or 'thin' accounts focus on the form and procedure of law: laws should be general, prospective, published, clear and stable, and applied by independent courts. Raz ('The Rule of Law and its Virtue', 1977) argued that the rule of law is one virtue a legal system may have, distinct from democracy or justice; a non-democratic system with unjust laws could in principle comply with it. Substantive or 'thick' accounts add content, especially protection of fundamental rights. Lord Bingham (The Rule of Law, 2010) included among his eight principles that the law must afford adequate protection of fundamental human rights and that the state must comply with its obligations in international law. The thin view is more precise and avoids turning the rule of law into a complete theory of justice; the thick view better matches how UK courts use the idea (e.g. access to justice in Unison), but at the cost of being more contested.

questions.q: Which case established that Parliament cannot bind its successors, because a later inconsistent Act impliedly repeals an earlier one?
options: Ellen Street Estates v Minister of Health
Thoburn v Sunderland City Council
R (Jackson) v Attorney General
Pickin v British Railways Board
questions.why: Ellen Street Estates [1934] (following Vauxhall Estates [1932]) applied implied repeal. Pickin concerns the enrolled bill rule; Thoburn limits implied repeal for constitutional statutes; Jackson concerns the Parliament Acts.

questions.q: What was decided in R (Jackson) v Attorney General [2005]?
options: The Lords' consent is always needed for constitutional legislation
The Hunting Act 2004 was invalid because the Parliament Act 1949 was delegated legislation
The Parliament Act 1949 and the Hunting Act 2004 were valid, with obiter doubts about absolute sovereignty
Courts may strike down Acts that breach the rule of law
questions.why: The House of Lords held the 1949 Act was primary legislation and valid, so the Hunting Act was valid. Comments about limits to sovereignty (Lords Steyn and Hope, Baroness Hale) were obiter; no Act was struck down.

questions.q: What is a 'constitutional statute', and what difference does the category make?
markScheme: Thoburn (Laws LJ, 2002): statutes conditioning the legal relationship between citizen and state or enlarging/diminishing fundamental rights
Examples: Magna Carta, Bill of Rights 1689, Acts of Union, ECA 1972, HRA 1998, devolution Acts
Cannot be impliedly repealed; only express words or words so specific that the inference of actual intention is irresistible
Endorsed in HS2 [2014] UKSC 3; applied in Allister [2023] (modification by clear words)
Evaluation: category is judge-made and its boundaries uncertain; does not limit Parliament's power to repeal expressly
questions.modelAnswer: In Thoburn v Sunderland City Council [2002], Laws LJ distinguished 'ordinary' from 'constitutional' statutes. A constitutional statute conditions the legal relationship between citizen and state in a general, overarching way, or enlarges or diminishes fundamental constitutional rights. Examples include Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights 1689, the Acts of Union, the European Communities Act 1972, the Human Rights Act 1998 and the devolution Acts. The significance is that such statutes cannot be impliedly repealed; a later Act affects them only through express words or words so specific that Parliament's intention is clear. The Supreme Court endorsed the idea in HS2 [2014], and in Allister [2023] accepted that the Acts of Union could be modified by clear words in EUWA s 7A. The category does not restrict Parliament's power to change such statutes expressly, and its boundaries remain uncertain.

questions.q: Why did the Supreme Court in Miller I [2017] hold that an Act of Parliament was needed to trigger Article 50?
options: Because the referendum was binding
Because withdrawal would change domestic law and remove statutory rights, which the prerogative cannot do
Because the devolved legislatures had a legal veto
Because treaties can never be made under the prerogative
questions.why: The prerogative cannot be used to change domestic law or remove rights created by Parliament. The referendum was advisory; the devolved legislatures had no legal veto (Sewel is a convention); treaties are normally made under the prerogative.

questions.q: What did the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 do?
options: Gave the CJEU jurisdiction over UK courts
Revoked all EU-derived law on 31 December 2023
Abolished the supremacy and general principles of EU law in domestic law from the end of 2023 and renamed retained EU law 'assimilated law'
Re-enacted the European Communities Act 1972
questions.why: The Act's original 'sunset' of all retained EU law was dropped; instead it revoked listed instruments, ended supremacy and general principles, and created the 'assimilated law' label. The ECA 1972 remains repealed; the CJEU has no general jurisdiction over UK courts.

questions.q: Explain how Factortame (No 2) was reconciled with parliamentary sovereignty.
markScheme: Factortame (No 2): House of Lords disapplied the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 for conflict with EU law
Lord Bridge: limitation of sovereignty was voluntarily accepted by Parliament in the ECA 1972
Explained as construction: s 2(4) ECA read into later Acts (later Acts take effect subject to EU law)
Alternative view (Wade): a 'revolution' changing the rule of recognition
Parliament retained power to repeal the ECA, as Brexit showed
questions.modelAnswer: In Factortame (No 2) [1991], the House of Lords granted relief disapplying parts of the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 that conflicted with EU law on freedom of establishment. Lord Bridge said that whatever limitation of sovereignty resulted was accepted voluntarily by Parliament when it enacted the European Communities Act 1972. One explanation is that s 2(4) of the ECA operated as a rule of construction, so later Acts were to take effect subject to directly effective EU law unless Parliament expressly said otherwise. H W R Wade argued that the decision was a 'technical revolution' changing the ultimate rule of recognition. Either way, Parliament kept the power to repeal the ECA, which it did through the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018.

questions.q: What is the legal status of the Sewel convention after Miller I?
options: It is a legally enforceable requirement of devolved consent
It is recognised in statute but is a political convention not enforceable by the courts
It was abolished by the Scotland Act 2016
It applies only to Northern Ireland
questions.why: Although s 28(8) of the Scotland Act 1998 (added in 2016) recognises it, the Supreme Court held it remains a political convention whose operation is not for the courts. It applies to all three devolved legislatures.

questions.q: Why was the Scottish Independence Referendum Bill outside the Scottish Parliament's competence?
options: Because Holyrood cannot hold any referendums
Because the Sewel convention was breached
Because the referendum would be legally binding
Because it related to reserved matters, namely the Union and the UK Parliament, even though it was advisory
questions.why: In [2022] UKSC 31 the Court held that even an advisory referendum on independence has more than a loose or consequential connection with the reserved matters of the Union and the UK Parliament. The Scottish Parliament can hold referendums on devolved matters; Sewel was not relevant.

questions.q: Compare the Scottish and Northern Irish devolution settlements.
markScheme: Scotland Act 1998: reserved powers model (Sch 5), single Scottish Parliament with broad powers, s 28(7) and Sewel, s 63A permanence
Northern Ireland Act 1998: excepted, reserved and transferred matters; based on Belfast/Good Friday Agreement
NI mandatory power-sharing (joint First Minister and deputy First Minister, cross-community voting)
NI principle of consent: s 1 border poll
NI institutions have collapsed/suspended repeatedly; Scotland stable but contested over independence
questions.modelAnswer: Both settlements use a model in which the devolved legislature may legislate on anything not expressly kept by Westminster. In Scotland, reserved matters are listed in Schedule 5 to the Scotland Act 1998. Westminster's power remains (s 28(7)), qualified politically by the Sewel convention (s 28(8)), and the institutions are declared permanent (s 63A). Northern Ireland's settlement under the Northern Ireland Act 1998 implements the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement. It divides matters into excepted, reserved and transferred categories, requires mandatory cross-community power-sharing (a jointly held First Minister and deputy First Minister office, and cross-community voting on key decisions), and enshrines the principle of consent (s 1). Northern Ireland's institutions have collapsed or been suspended several times, most recently from 2022 to 2024. Scotland's have been stable, but its constitutional debate centres on independence, which is reserved.

questions.q: Which case held that where a statute covers the same ground as a prerogative power, the prerogative is displaced?
options: CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service [1985]
BBC v Johns [1965]
Case of Proclamations (1611)
Attorney-General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel [1920]
questions.why: De Keyser held the Crown had to pay compensation under statute rather than requisition under the prerogative. Proclamations held the King cannot change the law; CCSU made prerogative reviewable; BBC v Johns said no new prerogatives can be created.

questions.q: In Miller II / Cherry [2019], which test did the Supreme Court apply to the prorogation of Parliament?
options: Whether the Prime Minister acted in bad faith
Whether the prorogation was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether it frustrated or prevented, without reasonable justification, Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions
Whether the Queen had personally approved it
questions.why: The Court defined the limits of the prerogative by reference to parliamentary sovereignty and accountability, and found no justification for a five-week prorogation. It did not need to find bad faith or apply Wednesbury.

questions.q: How effective is individual ministerial responsibility as a mechanism of accountability?
markScheme: Definition: ministers answer to Parliament for their departments and must not mislead it (Ministerial Code)
Distinguishes answerability (explaining) from culpability (resignation)
Resignations for departmental failure are rare; more often for personal conduct
Supporting mechanisms: questions, select committees, PAC, Ombudsman
Weaknesses: executive dominance of the Commons, Code enforced by PM; evaluation
questions.modelAnswer: Individual ministerial responsibility means ministers are answerable to Parliament for their departments and must give accurate and truthful information, correcting any inadvertent error; knowingly misleading Parliament is expected to lead to resignation (Ministerial Code). In practice, accountability now usually means answerability (explaining and putting things right) rather than resignation; resignations for departmental failings are rare, and most follow personal misconduct or political loss of support. The convention is supported by questions, select committee scrutiny (strengthened by elected chairs since 2010), the Public Accounts Committee and the Ombudsman. Its effectiveness is limited because the government usually controls the Commons and the Prime Minister decides whether the Ministerial Code has been breached. It works best as a duty to inform and explain rather than as a sanction.

questions.q: Which ground of judicial review is described by the test 'so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it'?
options: Illegality
Wednesbury irrationality
Procedural impropriety
Legitimate expectation
questions.why: This is Lord Greene MR's formulation in Wednesbury [1948]. Illegality concerns misunderstanding or exceeding powers; procedural impropriety concerns fairness and statutory procedure; legitimate expectation is a distinct fairness-based head.

questions.q: What is the test for apparent bias in English public law?
options: Whether there was a real danger of bias in the court's view
Whether the claimant reasonably suspected bias
Whether the decision-maker was actually biased
Whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias
questions.why: Porter v Magill [2001] adopted the fair-minded and informed observer test, modifying the 'real danger' test from Gough. Actual bias need not be proved; the claimant's subjective suspicion is not the test.

questions.q: Outline the procedural requirements a claimant must meet to bring a claim for judicial review in England and Wales.
markScheme: Claim under s 31 Senior Courts Act 1981 and CPR Part 54; permission required
Time: promptly and in any event within three months (CPR 54.5)
Standing: sufficient interest (s 31(3); National Federation; World Development Movement)
Amenability: public body or public function (Datafin)
Exhaust alternative remedies; s 31(2A)/(3C) 'highly likely not substantially different' may bar relief
questions.modelAnswer: A claim is made to the Administrative Court under s 31 of the Senior Courts Act 1981 and CPR Part 54, and the claimant needs permission. The claim must be brought promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds arising (CPR 54.5), with shorter limits in planning and procurement cases. The claimant must have a 'sufficient interest' (s 31(3)), which is assessed with the merits and has been interpreted generously for public interest groups (National Federation [1982]; World Development Movement [1995]). The decision must be amenable to review: made by a public body or in the exercise of a public function (Datafin [1987]). Claimants should normally use any suitable alternative remedy first. Finally, the court must refuse permission or relief if it is highly likely the outcome would not have been substantially different without the conduct complained of, unless there is an exceptional public interest (s 31(2A) and (3C)).

questions.q: What is the effect of a declaration of incompatibility under s 4 HRA 1998?
options: The government must repeal the provision within six months
The provision is struck down immediately
The provision remains valid and in force; it is for Parliament and government to respond
The provision must be read compatibly under s 3
questions.why: Section 4(6) provides that a declaration does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the provision. Section 3 interpretation is an alternative used first; there is no legal duty to amend, though s 10 remedial orders allow fast-track amendment.

questions.q: Which case used s 3 HRA to read 'as his or her wife or husband' as including same-sex partners?
options: R (Steinfeld) v Secretary of State [2018]
Bellinger v Bellinger [2003]
Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004]
questions.why: Ghaidan applied s 3 to the Rent Act 1977. Bellinger resulted in a s 4 declaration (gender recognition); Steinfeld in a declaration on civil partnerships; R v A (No 2) used s 3 on sexual history evidence.

questions.q: Distinguish the roles of ss 3, 4 and 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998.
markScheme: s 3: interpretive duty: read legislation compatibly 'so far as it is possible' (Ghaidan); limits (Re S)
s 4: if not possible, declaration of incompatibility; no effect on validity (s 4(6)); examples (Bellinger, A v SSHD)
s 6: public authorities must act compatibly; core and hybrid authorities; courts are public authorities
s 6(2): defence where primary legislation required the act
Link to sovereignty: Parliament has last word
questions.modelAnswer: Section 3 requires courts, so far as possible, to read and give effect to legislation compatibly with Convention rights. It is strong enough to read words in or down (Ghaidan [2004]), but cannot contradict a fundamental feature of the legislation (Re S [2002]). Where a compatible reading is impossible, s 4 allows the higher courts to make a declaration of incompatibility, which does not affect the provision's validity or operation (s 4(6)); Parliament decides how to respond, as after Bellinger [2003] (Gender Recognition Act 2004) and A v SSHD [2004]. Section 6 makes it unlawful for public authorities, including courts and hybrid bodies performing public functions, to act incompatibly with Convention rights, which gives individuals a cause of action. Section 6(2) protects an authority that could not have acted differently because of primary legislation. Together these provisions protect rights while leaving Parliament the final word.

questions.q: 'Parliamentary sovereignty remains the bedrock of the UK constitution; the challenges to it are political, not legal.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out Dicey's orthodox account and the enrolled bill and implied repeal rules (Pickin; Ellen Street)
EU membership: Factortame; explanations (construction under s 2(4) vs revolution); Brexit as reassertion of sovereignty
Common law constitutionalism: Jackson dicta, Privacy International, principle of legality, Anisminic
Constitutional statutes (Thoburn, HS2, Allister) as a modification of implied repeal
Devolution: s 28(7) legal power vs Sewel convention (Miller I) and political permanence (s 63A)
HRA: s 4(6) preserves sovereignty; political pressure to respond to declarations
Distinguishes legal from political constraints and evaluates whether courts would ever refuse to apply an Act
Reasoned conclusion engaging with the quotation
questions.modelAnswer:
Dicey defined parliamentary sovereignty as Parliament's right to make or unmake any law, with no person or body able to override or set aside its legislation. Courts apply the enrolled bill rule (Pickin [1974]) and the doctrine of implied repeal (Ellen Street Estates [1934]). On this account, sovereignty is a legal rule, and any limits are political: Parliament could legally legislate to abolish devolution or repeal the HRA, but would face political consequences.

Several developments test the claim. First, EU membership. In Factortame (No 2) [1991] the courts disapplied an Act of Parliament. Yet Lord Bridge presented this as a limitation Parliament voluntarily accepted in 1972, and Parliament later repealed the ECA. Brexit, confirmed by Miller I [2017] as requiring an Act of Parliament, can be read as a reassertion of sovereignty: Parliament joined, and Parliament left.

Second, common law constitutionalism. In Jackson [2005], Lords Steyn and Hope and Baroness Hale suggested obiter that courts might not apply an Act abolishing judicial review, and Lord Hope said the rule of law is the ultimate controlling factor. In Privacy International [2019], Lord Carnwath said the courts decide the rule-of-law limits on ouster clauses. Combined with Anisminic and the principle of legality (Simms), these suggest the courts will strain to interpret statutes to preserve fundamental principles. But no court has refused to apply clear words in an Act, so these remain potential rather than actual legal limits.

Third, constitutional statutes. Thoburn and HS2 hold that some statutes cannot be impliedly repealed. This alters the rule of implied repeal and is a genuine legal change, but it does not prevent express repeal, and Allister [2023] shows that clear words suffice even for the Acts of Union.

Fourth, devolution. Section 28(7) of the Scotland Act preserves Westminster's power, and Miller I held the Sewel convention is not legally enforceable, even though it is in statute. The permanence provision (s 63A) is likewise more political than legal. Here the quotation looks accurate: constraints on Westminster are strong but political.

Fifth, the HRA. Section 4(6) leaves Parliament free to ignore declarations of incompatibility, but in practice governments usually respond, creating a political constraint.

In conclusion, the quotation is broadly right as a description of current law: courts still apply Acts of Parliament, and most limits are political or interpretive. But it understates two things. The courts have developed interpretive tools (legality, constitutional statutes, the approach to ousters) that significantly shape what Parliament can achieve without very clear words, and senior judges have left open the possibility that some legislation would not be applied. Sovereignty remains the bedrock, but a bedrock that the courts now read in the light of the rule of law.

questions.q:
The (fictional) Public Spaces Act 2025 gives the Home Secretary power to 'make such orders restricting assemblies as she considers necessary for the prevention of serious public disorder'. The Home Secretary announces a policy of banning every assembly within 1 km of Parliament, without exception. Green Futures, a campaign group, applies for permission to hold a small silent vigil there. Its letter is rejected in a one-line reply citing the policy. Green Futures learns that a senior official involved in drafting the policy is a director of a company that has been the target of Green Futures' campaigns. Months earlier, the Home Office had publicly promised that 'peaceful, small-scale vigils will always be permitted'.
Advise Green Futures.
markScheme: Procedure: permission, promptness/three months, standing (sufficient interest for campaign group), amenability (statutory power of minister)
Illegality: fettering discretion by a rigid blanket policy; must consider individual cases
Illegality: improper purpose or irrelevant considerations if ban not related to serious disorder (Padfield)
Irrationality: blanket ban including silent vigils arguably Wednesbury unreasonable; intensity heightened as rights engaged
Procedural fairness: reasons and hearing (Doody); apparent bias test (Porter v Magill) on official's interest
Legitimate expectation from clear public promise (Coughlan); procedural or substantive; whether frustrating it is justified
HRA s 6 and Articles 10 and 11: interference must be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim and be proportionate (Bank Mellat); s 3 reading of the power
Remedies: quashing order, declaration, possibly mandatory order; s 31(2A) unlikely to bar relief
questions.modelAnswer:
Procedure. Green Futures should seek permission from the Administrative Court under s 31 of the Senior Courts Act 1981 and CPR Part 54, promptly and in any event within three months of the refusal. As a campaign group directly affected by the refusal, it has a sufficient interest (s 31(3)). The decision is made by a minister under statutory power, so it is clearly amenable to review.

Illegality. The Act requires the Home Secretary to judge what is 'necessary for the prevention of serious public disorder'. A policy is lawful in principle, but adopting a rigid rule that admits no exceptions and refusing to consider individual applications unlawfully fetters discretion. The one-line reply suggests no individual consideration. In addition, banning every assembly within 1 km, including silent vigils that pose no plausible risk of serious disorder, suggests the power is being used for a purpose beyond that for which it was conferred, or that irrelevant considerations (such as the political inconvenience of protests near Parliament) were taken into account (Padfield [1968]).

Irrationality. A blanket ban that captures harmless small vigils may be so unreasonable that no reasonable minister could adopt it (Wednesbury). Because freedom of expression and assembly are at stake, the court will apply more intense scrutiny (Kennedy; Pham).

Procedural impropriety. Fairness may require Green Futures to be able to make representations and to be given reasons, especially given the importance of the rights affected (Doody). On bias, the test is whether a fair-minded and informed observer, knowing the official's directorship of a company targeted by Green Futures, would conclude there was a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill [2001]). If the official influenced the policy as applied to Green Futures, the decision may be tainted.

Legitimate expectation. The Home Office's public statement that small peaceful vigils will always be permitted is clear, unambiguous and devoid of qualification. It creates at least a procedural expectation of consideration, and arguably a substantive one (Coughlan [2001]). The Home Secretary may depart from it only where that is a proportionate means of pursuing a legitimate aim, which requires some reasoned justification. None is apparent.

Human rights. The Home Secretary is a public authority (s 6 HRA), so she must act compatibly with Articles 10 (expression) and 11 (assembly). A ban interferes with these rights. It must be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim (prevention of disorder qualifies) and be proportionate under the Bank Mellat test. A blanket ban that includes silent vigils fails the 'less intrusive means' and 'fair balance' stages. Section 3 may be used to read the Act's power as permitting only proportionate restrictions, so there is no need for a declaration of incompatibility.

Remedies. The court could quash the refusal and possibly the policy, grant a declaration, and perhaps order reconsideration. Given the multiple flaws, it is unlikely that s 31(2A) (outcome highly likely to be the same) would bar relief. Green Futures has strong grounds, particularly fettering, legitimate expectation and Articles 10 and 11.
